title: Say where animating an icon and editing a video are the same job
goal: With both sets of flows on the table, work out honestly where they are one experience and where they only look like one. The answer decides whether the next year of this is one surface built once or two surfaces that happen to both involve time, and it should be written plainly enough that somebody can disagree with it.
notes:
Depends on the mocks existing. This is the task that actually answers the user's question, and its output is a recommendation plus a decision card, not code.

Be honest about the asymmetry rather than finding a tidy answer. Doing animation first plausibly accelerates video, because video would inherit a proven time and keyframe model. Doing video first does not accelerate animation, because nothing about codecs, audio or frame scheduling teaches you anything about emitting declarative SMIL. If the comparison finds the reverse, say so with the evidence; if it finds what is written here, say that too and do not dress it up as a surprise.

The trap to avoid is the tidy answer. Two flows can be drawn to look identical by drawing them vaguely. Where the mocks had to be vague to make two things match, that is a finding and belongs in the report.

---
SHARED CONTEXT for the animation and video alignment study (asked for by the user on 2026-09-14).

The user's words: "We also don't have usage clickthroughs for creating animated svgs so its unclear if anything could align with the clickthroughs of editing videos. We might want to figure out if there are opportunities to consolidate experience flows at all before building by mocking some flows up first and seeing how it will work. I want it to make sense for the user's usage scenario, and we might need different project types to isolate/hide some of the scenarios."

THIS IS A STUDY, NOT A BUILD. Nothing in this set changes Sources/. The deliverable is mocks and a written recommendation the user decides on. Do not start building a timeline, a keyframe model or a project type off the back of it; the whole point is to find out what to build before building it.

WHAT EXISTS, checked rather than assumed:
- Ten video clickthroughs under docs/design/mocks/pages: video-entry-wt, video-cut-wt, video-move-wt, video-zoom-wt, video-transition-wt, video-freeze-wt, video-title-wt, video-captions, video-compositing, video-speed.
- Six drawing ones: vector-wt, icon-draw-wt, icon-gradient-wt, draw, draw-boolean, iconography.
- ZERO for animating anything. The user is right: there is nothing to compare against.
- No project type concept in the app at all. A document is a canvas with a size (AppCoordinator.newBlankCanvasWindow(size:), File > New Blank Canvas). There is no kind, no template, nothing that hides one scenario's tools from another.
- Video today is a SEPARATE editor from the layer document: VideoEditorState and VideoEditorView, single clip, trim and crop and export. TrimTimeline and PlaybackScrubber are SwiftUI views bound to VideoEditorState, not a reusable time model, and PhotonzCore has no notion of time or keyframes at all. So the "shared foundation" is not something being reused; it is something that would have to be built, which is exactly why the user wants to look before leaping.

THE QUESTION UNDERNEATH, worth holding on to while mocking: the two things genuinely overlap in ONE place, a document that has a duration, a playhead and keyframes on properties. They diverge everywhere else. Video is sampled media: codecs, audio, frame scheduling, large data. Animated SVG is declarative: properties animate and the export emits SMIL or CSS and never rasterizes at all. A mock that pretends those are the same surface will look tidy and mislead everybody.

Conform to the shared mock library rather than inventing: docs/design/mocks/shared/UX-PATTERNS.md is the rulebook, docs/design/mocks/shared/AGENTS.md explains how pages are built, components/ holds the shared CSS and JS, and docs/design/mocks/dev-server.mjs serves them. A page that invents its own shell or its own controls cannot be compared with the video pages, which defeats the purpose.
acceptance: The animation flows and the video flows are laid out side by side, step for step, so the comparison can be seen rather than asserted
A written answer names what is genuinely the same job, what is superficially similar but different underneath, and what is unique to each
The answer covers at least: how time is shown and moved through, how a change over time is expressed, how you preview it, and how it leaves the app
Every claim that two things could be one thing is backed by both flows working with that one thing, shown in the mocks rather than argued in prose

The cost of consolidating is stated as plainly as the benefit, including what video would have to become: it is a separate single-clip editor today and sharing anything means it moves into the layer document
It says what to build FIRST and why, in a way the user can accept or reject in one read
A decision card is opened for the user with the real options and a recommendation, rather than the answer being taken for granted
Audit under queue/audits/ with the side-by-side, and anything rough filed as a follow-up
When the decision comes back answered, the study part of this task is already finished: the only act left is to turn the chosen option into the tasks that build it, then set this done

log.note: deps set: mock first, then compare, then decide

The five animation clickthroughs are built and pushed: icon-animate-wt, icon-loop-wt, icon-states-wt, icon-drawon-wt, icon-export-anim-wt, all in the Icons group of the mock index. You have something to compare now.

Three things to carry into the comparison, found while drawing them:

1) They overlap in exactly ONE place, and it is narrower than it looks. Icon keys are PERCENTAGES OF A CYCLE (0%, 50%, 100%) because a loop that repeats has no absolute time to sit on, and that is also literally what a CSS keyframe and a SMIL keyTimes are. Video keys are ABSOLUTE SECONDS on a document with a last frame. Those are not the same ruler and cannot share one.

2) Three of the four scenarios have no time axis at all. A spinner is one turn plus the word forever, so a ruler with an end cannot draw it. A toggle is two drawings and a crossing. Only the draw-on badge has an order in it, and two shapes in order came out as a two row list with numbers, not a track.

3) The consolidation worth having is probably NOT icons with video. It is icon states with COMPONENT VARIANTS: the same named list, the same differs-in-this-state count, the same crossing duration. Built separately they will drift. See icon-states-wt and pages/ui-variants.

AND THE GAP THIS STUDY LEAVES, which the comparison should decide: no page shows a WHOLE SET animating together, and that is exactly where the two row order list breaks down and a real timeline starts to earn its place. If the answer is a timeline, that is the case that proves it. Please widen this task to answer it rather than filing a near-twin.

left rough, not filed:
1) The screenshots in the audit are browser captures of the mock page, not app captures. This task changed nothing under Sources, so there was no build to photograph and no playtest walk to take a -sc.png from. No task: there is nothing to fix.
2) The destination-first export sheet is the one 'these could be one thing' claim not proved on both sides: it exists on the icon side and nowhere on the video side, where all ten flows export with one button and no questions. A task to draw it on a video flow would serve the video-editing epic, which is staged later, so per the staging rule it is not filed. The page says so in place instead.
3) The consolidation the study thinks is actually worth having, icon states with component variants (icon-states-wt vs ui-variants), is a design proposal rather than a defect, and speculative features get validated before they get built. It is an evaluate question on the audit so the user can turn it into a task if they want it.
4) The page is long. Eight comparison rows, three proof pairs, two rulers and two forms of the multi-part case are each an acceptance item, so the length is the deliverable, but a reader gets the answer in the first paragraph and everything after it is evidence.

Filed as its own task: one-set-of-easing-curves-named-the-same-way-ever (four different easing vocabularies live across six mock pages, reproduced with the exact grep and its output; the design language already names exactly three curves in tokens.css and none of the six controls maps onto them).
Folded into an existing task: work-out-whether-the-app-needs-project-types-at now carries this study's answer on project types.

Adversarial review, before building the page: the trap named in the notes was real and the page is shaped around avoiding it. The tidy answer here is 'both are documents with a duration, a playhead and keyframes, so build one timeline', and it survives only if you never write down what a spinner is. Three of the four icon scenarios have no end in them, so the page leads with the negative result and makes the reader look at two rulers rather than read a sentence about them. The one place the mocks WERE vague to make two things match is named on the page in place: the destination-first export sheet is drawn on the icon side and nowhere on the video side, so the video half of that pair is this page's proposal rather than a quotation, and it is labelled the weakest of the three.

Adversarial review, on the built page: fixed two things found by using it. At narrow widths the Verdict column header was orphaned onto its own half-row, because it is the 4th CHILD of the grid and the media query had hidden :last-child, which is a different element. And 'repeats forever' parked inside the cycle strip covered the 100% key, which is the one key that block exists to point at, so it moved outside the strip where it also reads better: the cycle is one pass and the loop is what happens after it. Checked at 1280 and at 880 with no horizontal overflow, and the shell loads it with the nav entry active. All five mock gates pass (check-reserved, check-a11y-names, check-fieldwrap, check-states, check-selection, check-elevation, check-shortcuts).

No Sources/ change, so no swift build, no Scripts/test.sh and no walks were needed or run.

Study delivered and a decision card is open for the user. The side-by-side is at docs/design/mocks/pages/time-compare.html (Icons > Animation vs video: the same job?), the long form at docs/design/animation-vs-video.md, the audit at queue/audits/2026-09-14-animation-vs-video.json. The answer: three shared controls, five surfaces that only look shared, and a ruler they cannot share because an icon repeats and a video finishes. Recommendation is to build motion as a property of a layer with no ruler at all. Waiting only on which of the four options the user picks; option d retires this task.

The decision card this is blocked on is premature: its recommended option a is 'pick a named motion like Pulse or Spin or Draw on', which is the assumption the user rejected on 2026-09-14 ('a fixed list of animations ... super weird and proprietary'). Do not treat the card as settled direction. The mocks are being redone on a per-property model (mock-animating-any-property-of-a-layer-with-the); re-frame the options against those pages, and keep the finding that stands on its own: an icon repeats and a video finishes, so they cannot share one ruler.

decision "Animating an icon and editing a video: one surface or two?" resolved: Motion is a property, and it opens into a cycle strip (Answered by the user in conversation on 2026-09-14, with one correction that overrides the option text. They said motion needs 'a much more consistent way to animate various properties similar to applying effects to a layer. But it should be applied to a timeline that is bigger than the property panel.' That is option b's shape: motion as a property of a layer, opening into a strip with a lane per moving part. The correction: the option text says 'pick a named motion like Pulse or Spin or Draw on', and the user rejected exactly that as 'super weird and proprietary'. There is NO canned list of motions. A person picks a PROPERTY to animate (position, scale, rotation with a movable origin, opacity, colour, path data, stroke), with named easing curves plus a custom one, and two parts of one icon must be able to carry the same motion out of phase. The bell that swings from a pivot at its top with a knob that lags is the test. Option a is dead because it has no ruler and the user asked for a surface with width; option c is not chosen, so video stays where it is for now. See the task mock-animating-any-property-of-a-layer-with-the for the full correction.)

2026-09-15 the premise this card is built on has been rejected by the user and the mocks it cites have been rebuilt. Recommended option a is 'pick a named motion like Pulse or Spin or Draw on', and the whole first round of icon animation mocks framed motion that way. The user's critique on 2026-09-14 called that 'super weird and proprietary'. The replacement is icon-animate-wt (Make a bell swing) and icon-phase-wt (Make the knob lag the bell): you animate a PROPERTY, the timing sits on a bottom dock with real width, and a lag between two parts is set by dragging one bar against another. ALSO: pages/time-compare.html, which is the evidence this card leans on, still argues the old model (icon timing is 'one field, typed, never dragged'; an Order list beats a track) and now contradicts the two new pages. It needs redoing before this card can be answered honestly. Do not resolve this card against the current option text.
